items.prompt: What is a 'module,' as this unit defines it?
choices: A single file that explicitly declares what it needs from other files and what it makes available to them
Any JavaScript file, regardless of whether it uses import/export
A file that must be loaded before all other files
A minified version of a JavaScript file
items.explanation: A module explicitly states its dependencies (import) and its exports, replacing the implicit ordering and shared globals that plain script tags rely on.
items.reference:
Module
explicitly declares what it needs (import)
explicitly declares what it provides (export)

Why: Explicit declarations are what let a tool compute a correct order automatically, instead of relying on manual bookkeeping.

items.prompt: How does a module system differ from plain `<script>` tags in how dependencies are expressed?
choices: A module system uses explicit import/export declarations; plain script tags rely on load order and shared global variables
There's no real difference — both approaches work identically
Plain script tags are actually more explicit about dependencies
A module system requires every file to be in a single directory
items.explanation: Plain script tags depend entirely on the order they're placed on the page; modules make the actual dependency relationship explicit and machine-readable.
items.reference:
Module
explicitly declares what it needs (import)
explicitly declares what it provides (export)

Why: Explicit declarations are what let a tool compute a correct order automatically, instead of relying on manual bookkeeping.

items.prompt: What is a 'dependency graph'?
choices: The full set of 'this module needs that module' relationships across a codebase, starting from one or more entry points
A visual chart showing a website's page navigation structure
A list of every function defined in a project
A performance graph showing page load times
items.explanation: The dependency graph captures exactly which modules need which other modules — this is what a bundler walks to compute a valid build order.
items.reference:
Dependency graph
module → its dependencies
starts from one or more entry points

Why: Without an explicit graph, there's no reliable way to compute a correct load order automatically.

items.prompt: Where does a bundler start when building a dependency graph?
choices: One or more entry points, following import statements outward from there
Alphabetically, from the first filename in the project directory
Randomly, checking every file in the project simultaneously
From the largest file in the project, by byte size
items.explanation: Starting from an entry point and following imports outward is what lets a bundler discover every module actually reachable — and, by extension, everything that isn't.
items.reference:
Dependency graph
module → its dependencies

items.prompt: What does a bundler actually do, per this unit's definition?
choices: Reads a dependency graph from an entry point and produces one (or a few) output files with every module included exactly once, in a valid order
Deletes unused files from a project directory
Compresses images to reduce file size
Runs a project's test suite automatically before every commit
items.explanation: A bundler's core job is graph resolution: walking dependencies from an entry point and producing correctly-ordered, deduplicated output.
items.reference:
Bundler
reads the dependency graph from an entry point
outputs modules exactly once, in valid order

Why: "Fewer files" is the visible effect — graph resolution is the actual mechanism producing it.

items.prompt: Why does a bundler ensure each module appears exactly once in its output, rather than once per script tag that references it?
choices: Because it tracks which modules it has already included while walking the graph, avoiding duplication or omission
Because JavaScript files are physically incapable of being included twice
Because bundlers always alphabetize output files, which coincidentally prevents duplication
Because browsers automatically deduplicate any repeated script content
items.explanation: The bundler's traversal explicitly tracks visited modules, which is the mechanism that guarantees exactly-once inclusion — nothing about JavaScript itself provides this automatically.
items.reference:
Bundler
reads the dependency graph from an entry point
outputs modules exactly once, in valid order

Why: "Fewer files" is the visible effect — graph resolution is the actual mechanism producing it.

items.prompt: What is transpilation?
choices: Converting source code written in a newer or non-standard syntax into equivalent code a target environment can actually run
Combining multiple files into a single output file
Removing unused code from a bundle
Compressing JavaScript to reduce its file size
items.explanation: Transpilation rewrites syntax, not files — it's a distinct problem from bundling, even though the two commonly run together in modern build tools.
items.reference:
Transpilation
rewrites syntax for compatibility
a different problem from bundling

Why: Bundling combines files correctly; transpilation makes syntax runnable — a project can genuinely need only one of the two.

Yes, they're two names for exactly the same process
Yes, but transpilation only applies to CSS files, not JavaScript

items.explanation: They solve genuinely different problems and just happen to run together in most modern build pipelines — a project could need bundling without transpilation, or vice versa.
